title: Does public-key encryption imply oblivious transfer?
formal: In the classical plain model, does the existence of an IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption scheme for bits imply the existence of a polynomial-time 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious-transfer protocol secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party? Both primitives have negligible error and computational security as defined below. The implication may use arbitrary non-black-box techniques and a polynomial number of communication rounds.
definitions: The security parameter is λ, supplied in unary. Honest algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; adversarial distinguishers are polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0, μ(λ)<λ^(−c) for all sufficiently large λ. Public-key encryption consists of KeyGen(1^λ)=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,m;r), and Dec(sk,c), for m∈{0,1}; decryption fails with negligible probability over key generation and encryption coins, for each m. IND-CPA means that no such adversary given pk distinguishes Enc(pk,0) from Enc(pk,1) with nonnegligible advantage; public encryption is available to it. In OT, sender S has bits (m_0,m_1), receiver R has a choice bit c, and R must output m_c except with negligible probability for every input triple; S has no output. The parties follow their prescribed algorithms but keep their entire views, including inputs, random tapes, and messages. There must be uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators Sim_S(1^λ,m_0,m_1) and Sim_R(1^λ,c,m_c) whose outputs are computationally indistinguishable from the corresponding real views for every sequence of input triples. Thus S learns nothing about c and R learns nothing beyond (c,m_c). The parties have independent private randomness and exchange classical messages directly. There is no trusted setup, common reference string, random oracle, pre-shared correlated randomness, trusted hardware, or quantum resource.
answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without a second unproved hardness assumption, or refute that unrelativized implication. A construction may inspect and use the code of the encryption algorithms and use non-black-box security arguments. An oracle separation or a lower bound restricted to black-box reductions is a barrier, not a negative resolution of this question. A construction requiring an additional property of encryption must also derive that property from arbitrary IND-CPA encryption to settle the card.
context:
Ordinary encryption protects a message from someone who lacks the secret key. Oblivious transfer must arrange a more selective situation: the receiver can read one of two messages, cannot read the other, and does not disclose which one it selected. This combines privacy for both participants. Merely encrypting both messages under a key generated by the receiver fails, because that receiver can decrypt both ciphertexts. Asking the receiver to reveal which key it can decrypt would instead reveal its choice.

Some encryption schemes offer the missing structure. If a receiver can create two indistinguishable-looking public keys while knowing a decryption key for just one, it can place the decryptable key in position c. The sender encrypts the two messages under the corresponding keys. Such an argument needs a suitable oblivious-sampling property, including security even given the sampler’s retained randomness. Gertner and coauthors identify sufficient properties and also prove an oracle separation between general PKE and even semi-honest OT. Their historical separation uses uniform adversaries.

That result constrains a style of construction, rather than deciding the unrestricted implication. In an oracle argument all algorithms are given access to an additional idealized operation. A construction based on the actual implementation of an encryption scheme may use features that do not survive replacement by an arbitrary oracle. Consequently, the qualifier allowing non-black-box techniques is substantive; removing it would turn the card into a question already addressed by known barriers.

The semi-honest target is already powerful. Haitner, Ishai, Kushilevitz, Lindell, and Petrank show how to transform semi-honest OT into OT secure against malicious parties, and obtain general secure computation without an honest majority. Their result fixes static corruption and standalone security; it does not promise fairness or guaranteed output delivery against a party that aborts. This explains why the basic passive-security implication matters without building stronger composition or fairness requirements into the question.

Progress continues through additional algebraic or sampling structure. Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE: anyone with the public key can turn a ciphertext into a fresh encryption of the same plaintext. This avoids their predecessors’ oblivious-sampling requirement but introduces a different hypothesis. Ordinary IND-CPA security alone does not include a public rerandomization algorithm.

A 2026 journal paper by Tanishita and coauthors studies updatable encryption, where update tokens let a third party transform ciphertexts across keys. With specified oblivious-sampling properties, it derives two- or three-round OT. Those theorems refine the boundary for a structured encryption primitive. They do not give a transformation starting with an arbitrary public-key encryption scheme.

A related barrier concerns fair coin tossing. Maji and Wang show limits for protocols using public-key encryption or key agreement as black boxes, whereas OT supports optimally fair constructions. This gives another operational way to see the distinction between ordinary encrypted communication and primitives complete for secure computation. The fairness result has its own model and does not constitute a proof against all non-black-box OT constructions.
why: Determines whether the ability to send secrets to a designated receiver already suffices for general private computation between mutually distrustful parties. It is a basic boundary in the hierarchy of cryptographic assumptions, with a longstanding black-box barrier and no known unrestricted implication.

importance.reason: A foundational comparison between ordinary public-key confidentiality and a primitive complete for secure computation; resolving it would change which assumptions suffice for a broad range of protocols.

progress.text: Gertner and coauthors prove an oracle with PKE but no semi-honest OT, and give positive constructions when PKE has specified extra properties. Their oracle separations use uniform adversaries.
Haitner and coauthors give a fully black-box compiler from semi-honest to malicious OT and general secure computation, establishing the strength of even the passive-security target.
Maji and Wang prove limitations on optimal fair coin tossing from black-box PKE or key agreement; this is further evidence about restricted constructions, not an unrestricted separation.
Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE, replacing oblivious sampling with a public ciphertext-rerandomization requirement.
The journal version of Tanishita and coauthors’ work derives OT from updatable encryption with additional sampling properties. It does not remove all extra assumptions on the starting primitive.

status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No unrestricted classical implication from arbitrary IND-CPA public-key encryption to OT was identified. Known oracle/black-box separations and positive results for rerandomizable or suitably samplable encryption do not settle this formulation. The card fixes semi-honest standalone security with classical communication and no setup.
